catalog_quote: 3.5. Die Betonung 3.5.1. Für die altaramäische Betonung, ihre Intensität, ihre Lage und ihre Veränderungen können aus den direkt auf uns gekommenen Texten nur einige Indizien festgestellt werden. Die Angaben der Betonung in den Bibeltexten mit babylonischer Punktation und die noch präziseren in den mit tiberischer Punktation erlauben, eine Reihe von Regeln festzustellen, deren Konsistenz und Konsequenz zwar sehr bedeutend sind, deren Realität aber von der Verläßlichkeit der masoretischen Überlieferung überhaupt abhängt. 3.5.2. Nach der masoretischen tiberischen Überlieferung tragen die meisten aramäischen Wörter den Hauptton auf der letzten Silbe, [p. 103] während dann der Hauptton auf der vorletzten Silbe (Pänultima) nur bei einigen Wortklassen und -formen vorkommt.

new_statements.translation: 3.5.1. For Old Aramaic stress - its intensity, its position and its changes - only a few indications can be established from the texts that have come down to us directly. [...] 3.5.2. According to the Masoretic Tiberian tradition most Aramaic words carry the main stress on the last syllable, whereas main stress on the next-to-last syllable (penult) occurs only in some word classes and forms. (Omitted middle sentence: the stress indications of the Babylonian- and, more precisely, Tiberian-pointed Bible texts allow a set of rules to be established whose consistency is significant but whose reality depends on the reliability of the Masoretic tradition.)

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is not recoverable from the unvocalised Old Aramaic/Sam'alian inscriptions beyond a few indirect indications (chiefly plene vs defective spelling of final long vowels, cf. Folmer 2011:132, Cook 1990). The rule the grammar states is the one transmitted by the Tiberian reading tradition of Biblical Aramaic and generally projected onto earlier Aramaic: main stress on the final syllable in most words, penultimate stress confined to specified word classes/forms. Creason 2004 (CEWAL sec. 3.5) gives the matching reconstruction: after the very early loss/lengthening of final short vowels, final (closed) syllables carried the stress and 'these rules remain unaltered throughout most of the history of Aramaic'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said for Old Aramaic (Segert speaks only of 'Hauptton').
new_statements.exceptions: Penultimate main stress 'nur bei einigen Wortklassen und -formen' (enumerated for Biblical Aramaic in Segert 3.5.3; 3.5.3.5 notes forms that 'retain the original stress on the penult'). In the Beyer/Folmer/Cook reconstruction, OA words with unstressed final long vowels (e.g. ʾnḥn /ʾanáḥnā/ 'we', written defectively) are penult-stressed.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level main stress ('Hauptton' of the word). The positive rule is that of a much later reading tradition (Tiberian Biblical Aramaic) plus comparative reconstruction, not an observation on olda1245 forms; Segert explicitly limits what the inscriptions themselves show to 'einige Indizien'. Extinct, consonantal-script corpus language.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog olda1245 lumps the Old Aramaic inscriptional dialects (Sefire, Zincirli/Sam'al, Tell Fekheriye etc.). None of the opened sources treats Sam'alian stress separately. Segert 1975 is a grammar of 'Altaramäisch' in the wide sense (early inscriptions 'AA' + Imperial + Biblical Aramaic); his positive stress rule (3.5.2) is explicitly that of the Tiberian Masoretic reading tradition of Biblical Aramaic (Glottolog files BA under Imperial Aramaic, impe1235), while for the early inscriptions themselves (the olda1245 corpus) he says only 'einige Indizien' are recoverable. Creason 2004 and Kaufman 1997 are pan-Aramaic sketches. Note the sibling impe1235 was judged not determinable in on the same evidential basis (unvocalised script; stress only reconstructed) — the editor may want to treat olda1245 consistently.

sources.note: 'There is one primary stressed syllable in each Aramaic word (with the exception of some particles..). In Proto-Aramaic, words having a final closed syllable were stressed on that syllable; and words having a final open syllable were stressed on the penultimate syllable, regardless of the length of the word-final vowel. At a very early stage, word-final short vowels were either lost or lengthened and so the stressed, open penultimate syllable of words with a final short vowel became the final stressed, closed syllable. sources.note: No stress section (3.1 Vowels, 3.2 Consonants, 3.3 Later sound changes only). Sole remark, p.132: defective vs plene spelling of final long vowels in OA/IA 'may be connected with word stress: unstressed final long vowels in a number of cases were written without a vowel letter.., whereas stressed long final vowels were normally written with a vowel letter (e.g. ʾnḥn for /ʾanaḥnā/ 'we')', citing Beyer ATTM 1:88 and Cook 1990 — i.e. stress position in OA is a reconstruction (final vs penult depending on form), not described.

sources.note: For Old Aramaic only: '*malkatu > malkat > malkah suggests that final unstressed vowels had dropped by this period.' For the later (Classical) dialects: 'The vocalization traditions indicate that by now (i.e. after the loss of final case vowels) stress was generally on the final syllable of the word, though the modern dialects (and some reading traditions) show a strong tendency toward penultimate stress.'
